title: Packet Analysis Field Notes: tcpdump, Wireshark & Reading the Wire
summary: A dense 10-page study-notes carousel covering packet capture fundamentals, tcpdump BPF filters, Wireshark capture/display workflows, dissecting TCP conversations and handshake timing, and decoding the TLS handshake from raw captures.

chapters.title: 1 · Packet Analysis Fundamentals
points: What a packet capture is: a copy of frames as they traverse an interface, snarfed before kernel processing (libpcap on Linux/macOS, Npcap on Windows)
Promiscuous vs non-promiscuous mode: promiscuous captures frames not addressed to you; monitor mode is for Wi-Fi 802.11 frames, a different beast entirely
Frame anatomy: Ethernet header → IP header → TCP header → payload; each layer is parsed by a dissector
Capture filters (BPF) run in-kernel and drop uninteresting packets early; display filters run post-capture on decoded fields — know which one you're writing
Snap length (-s): truncating payloads saves disk but breaks TLS/TCP reassembly; full capture needs snaplen 0 (or 262144)
Ring buffers (-C filesize -W filecount) keep captures bounded on long-running boxes
Where to capture matters: on the client, on the server, or in between — NAT, offload, and asymmetry change what you see
Checksum offload gotcha: packets leaving the NIC show bad checksums locally; disable offload or ignore those errors
Capturing requires privileges: root or CAP_NET_RAW on Linux; expect 'you don't have permission' without it
The follow-the-conversation mindset: packets are noise, conversations (flows) are the signal
Timestamps are everything for latency work: verify clock sync (NTP) on hosts before trusting inter-packet deltas
Rule of thumb: filter early (capture), analyze late (display), never grep a 10 GB pcap

chapters.title: 2 · tcpdump Essentials
points: Basic usage: tcpdump -i eth0 -n (no DNS lookups — faster, less traffic), -nn for ports too, -v/-vv/-vvv for decoding depth
Write to file: tcpdump -w out.pcap; read back with -r out.pcap; combine with -A or -X to dump ASCII/hex payloads
Host filters: host 10.0.0.5, src host, dst host; net 10.0.0.0/8 for subnets
Port filters: port 443, src port 53, dst port 80; 'portrange 6000-6010' for a spread
Protocol & primitives: tcp, udp, icmp, arp, ip6; combine with and/or/not and parentheses (escape them in shells)
'tcp[13] & 2 != 0' — raw BPF on TCP flags byte to match SYN packets; classic interview filter
Quantifiers: less 100, greater 1500 (byte lengths); 'ether broadcast', 'ip multicast'
Limit count: -c 100 stops after 100 packets — perfect for quick sanity captures
Verbosity timing: use -ttttt for microsecond deltas between packets (absolute time deltas)
Common mistake: forgetting -n turns every packet into DNS lookups, polluting your own capture
tcpdump shows SYN, but retransmission detection is painful by hand — capture wide, then analyze in Wireshark
Recipe: tcpdump -i any -nn -s0 -w cap.pcap 'tcp port 443 and host api.example.com'

chapters.title: 3 · BPF Filters Deep Dive
points: BPF (Berkeley Packet Filter) compiles your filter expression to bytecode executed in-kernel — unmatched packets never cross the syscall boundary
Check compiled output: tcpdump -d '<expr>' prints the bytecode; -dd/-ddd give C/decimal forms
Primitive grammar: [proto] [dir] type value — e.g., 'src net', 'dst port', 'ether host'
Byte-access syntax: proto[expr:size] — tcp[0:2] is the source port, ip[2:2] is total length
Flag arithmetic: tcp[tcpflags] & (tcp-syn|tcp-fin) != 0 matches SYN or FIN without counting byte offsets by hand
Named offsets: tcp-syn, tcp-ack, tcp-fin, tcp-rst, tcp-push — prefer them over magic numbers
VLAN gotcha: tagged frames shift the Ethernet header — use 'vlan and tcp port 443' or offsets break
IPv6 caveat: 'ip proto tcp' misses IPv6; use 'ip6 protochain 6' or plain 'tcp' which matches both
Filter for TCP problems: 'tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-rst != 0' isolates resets — the fastest way to find refused connections
Complex filters get slow on busy boxes: pre-narrow with host/port before byte tests
tcpdump -G 3600 -w cap_%H.pcap rotates hourly when paired with -w and strftime-style names
Debug trick: if a filter matches nothing, drop to the broadest primitive and re-add terms one at a time

chapters.title: 4 · Wireshark Workflows
points: Capture options: choose interface, enable capture filter, set ring buffer for long captures; the double-click filter field is your BPF syntax check
Display filters vs capture filters: display uses dot-notation (ip.addr == 10.0.0.5), capture uses BPF (host 10.0.0.5) — different grammars, never mix
Essential display filters: tcp.stream eq 5, http.request, tls.handshake.type == 1, tcp.analysis.retransmission
Filter shortcuts: right-click a field → Apply as Filter / Prepare as Filter; Learn display filters from the packet bytes pane
Follow → Follow TCP Stream: reassembles a flow into readable request/response; 'Follow → Save as' exports one side
Statistics menu: Conversations (bytes/packets per flow), Endpoints, Protocol Hierarchy, I/O Graph
Protocol Hierarchy first: on any unknown pcap, it shows what's on the wire and where the anomalies concentrate
I/O Graph: plot bits/s or filtered traffic over time; spot throughput cliffs and retransmission storms visually
Coloring rules: green = TCP, gold = TLS, red = RST/errors — decode at a glance before filtering anything
Mark & ignore: mark packets (M) for a shortlist, ignore noisy chatter (N) to shrink analysis surface
Expert Information (Analyze → Expert Info): aggregated warnings — retransmissions, zero window, malformed — the triage panel
Keyboard flow: Ctrl-F to search packets, / to filter, Ctrl+Shift+C to colorize a conversation

chapters.title: 5 · Reading TCP Conversations
points: A conversation = 4-tuple (src IP:port, dst IP:port); Wireshark assigns each a stream index you filter on with tcp.stream eq N
Normal lifecycle: SYN → SYN/ACK → ACK (handshake) → data/PUSH → FIN or RST teardown
Follow TCP Stream shows client in red, server in blue; toggle 'Show data as' raw/ASCII/hex for binary protocols
Sequence numbers: Wireshark shows relative sequence numbers by default — disable in TCP preferences to see raw 32-bit ISNs
Retransmission: same sequence number seen again; Wireshark flags it via tcp.analysis.retransmission (and fast_retransmission)
Duplicate ACK = receiver signaling a gap; 3 dup-ACKs trigger fast retransmit before RTO fires
Zero window: receiver advertises window 0 — an application-not-reading problem, not a network one
TCP reset mid-stream: no FIN, conversation dies with RST — usually firewall, timeout kill, or crashed peer
MTU/fragmentation clues: 'TCP segment of a reassembled PDU' and 'length > MSS' point at path MTU trouble
Out-of-order vs retransmission: out-of-order = late but ordered arrival; retransmission = never arrived — different root causes
Statistics → Conversations sorted by duration finds long-lived flows; sorted by bytes finds the heavy hitters
Habit: label streams in Notes (Ctrl+M bookmarks) so a 2-hour investigation is re-readable tomorrow

chapters.title: 6 · SYN/ACK Timing & Latency
points: TCP handshake timing is a free RTT probe: SYN→SYN/ACK delta ≈ server-side RTT (plus backlog queueing)
SYN sent → SYN/ACK received: network round trip + accept queue processing — measure with frame.time_delta (Wireshark) or tcpdump -ttttt
SYN/ACK → ACK: client processing time, usually sub-millisecond; if not, client CPU is suspect
ACK → first data byte: application latency — server accepted but app is slow to respond
Wireshark: io,stat with frame.time_delta filter, or tcp.analysis.initial_rtt per stream; Statistics → TCP Stream Graphs → Round Trip Time
SYN with no SYN/ACK: packet dropped (ACL, asymmetric routing) or server backlog full — retransmitted SYNs at 1s/2s/4s backoff are the fingerprint
SYN → RST: port closed or firewall reject; distinguish from silent drop (nothing comes back)
Half-open connections: many SYNs without completion suggest SYN flood or accept-queue exhaustion (somaxconn/backlog)
Cloud gotcha: captures inside VMs miss hypervisor drops — SYN seen but never answered may die between host and wire
Intercontinental baseline: ~100 ms RTT coast-to-coast US, ~250 ms transpacific; know the floor before blaming the app
TCP timestamps option gives RTT samples on every packet, not just handshake — more robust for steady-state latency
Compare handshake time across captures at client AND server: client-side delta minus server-side delta ≈ one-way network

chapters.title: 7 · The TLS Handshake in Captures
points: TLS 1.2: ClientHello → ServerHello + Certificate + ServerHelloDone → ClientKeyExchange + ChangeCipherSpec → Finished — 2 round trips
TLS 1.3: ClientHello → ServerHello + {EncryptedExtensions, Certificate, Finished} → client Finished — 1 RTT, everything after ServerHello is encrypted
Filter handshake messages: tls.handshake.type == 1 (ClientHello), == 2 (ServerHello), == 11 (Certificate), == 12 (ServerKeyExchange)
ClientHello reveals: SNI (server name), cipher suites offered, ALPN (h2 vs http/1.1), supported versions — filter tls.handshake.extensions_server_name
Version negotiation: legacy_version + supported_versions extension; TLS 1.3 looks like 1.2 in the header — read the extension
Certificate chain in the clear (TLS ≤1.2): Wireshark shows issuer, SANs, validity — instant way to spot expired/mismatched certs
TLS 1.3 certificate encryption: server cert is inside encrypted extensions — you must decrypt to see it
ChangeCipherSpec in TLS 1.3 is a compatibility shim — its presence doesn't mean an old version
Failed handshakes: handshake_failure (cipher mismatch), certificate_unknown, alert encrypted after ClientHello in 1.3
Session resumption: session tickets / PSK shrink the handshake — resumed 1.3 connections send data in the first flight
Filter alerts: tls.alert_message.desc != 0; filter all TLS to one IP: tls.handshake and ip.addr == x
Diagnostic habit: ClientHello sent but no ServerHello = middlebox drop or SNI-based blocking; ServerHello but stalls = key exchange/MTU issue

chapters.title: 8 · Decrypting TLS & Keylog Files
points: SSLKEYLOGFILE: browsers and curl (libcurl) write per-session secrets to this env var; point Wireshark at it via Preferences → Protocols → TLS
Keylog format: one line per secret — CLIENT_HANDSHAKE_TRAFFIC_SECRET <client_random> <hex>
What decrypts: full HTTP/2 or HTTP/1.1 plaintext, extension details, certificates in TLS 1.3 — but only sessions whose keys you captured
Cannot decrypt without keys: ECDHE gives forward secrecy — a stolen server private key won't unlock old captures
RSA key exchange (legacy): Wireshark can decrypt with the server's private key alone (Preferences → TLS → RSA keys list)
Gotcha: ECDHE_RSA ciphers make RSA-key decryption fail silently — check the key exchange actually used in ServerKeyExchange
Decrypting server-side with OpenSSL s_server or NGINX SSLKEYLOGFILE support for controlled test captures
After enabling keylog: restart the browser — secrets only log for NEW sessions, resumed sessions need their tickets too
Verify decryption worked: 'Decrypted TLS' tab appears in the byte pane; http2 frames appear in the packet list
Privacy/compliance: keylog files are live credentials — never commit them; rotate and delete after analysis
Trace-level alternative: eBPF/strace on the app shows plaintext before encryption — sometimes easier than capture decryption
Workflow recap: set SSLKEYLOGFILE → reproduce issue in browser → capture with tcp.port == 443 → open pcap + keylog in Wireshark

chapters.title: 9 · Common Mistakes & Triage Patterns
points: Mistake: capturing without -s0 (or snaplen) — truncated TLS records and HTTP headers you can't dissect
Mistake: trusting timestamps from unsynced hosts; deltas across machines are meaningless without NTP
Mistake: filtering display vs capture syntax interchangeably — 'host x' in a display filter box matches nothing
Mistake: analyzing only one side of the conversation — always compare client-side and server-side captures of the same window
Mistake: chasing checksum errors caused by NIC offload instead of real corruption
Pattern — slow page load: capture, sort by tcp.time_delta descending, find the biggest gaps, map each gap to request/app/RTT
Pattern — intermittent failure: long ring-buffer capture + tcp.analysis.flags display filter to surface retransmits/RSTs when they happen
Pattern — connection refused vs dropped: RST back = reachable-but-refusing; silence = ACL/routing/blackhole
Pattern — high handshake latency: SYN→SYN/ACK big on both captures = network; big only server-side = accept queue/app
Tool laddering: tcpdump to capture wide and cheap → tshark for scripted extraction (tshark -r x.pcap -Y 'filter' -T fields) → Wireshark GUI for the deep dive
SplitRcap/mergecap: cut huge pcaps to the relevant window before opening the GUI — Wireshark chokes past a few hundred MB
Always document: which host, interface, filter, start/end time — a pcap without provenance is an unsolvable puzzle

chapters.title: 10 · Cheat Sheet & Closing Summary
points: Capture recipe: tcpdump -i any -nn -s0 -w cap.pcap 'tcp port 443 and host api.example.com'
Problem isolators: 'tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-rst != 0' (resets), 'tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-syn != 0 and tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-ack == 0' (bare SYNs)
Wireshark power filters: tcp.stream eq N, tcp.analysis.retransmission, tls.handshake.type == 1, tls.handshake.extensions_server_name contains "example"
Wireshark stats flow: Protocol Hierarchy → Conversations → I/O Graph → Expert Info → Follow Stream — run it in that order every time
Timing rules: SYN→SYN/ACK ≈ RTT; ACK→first data ≈ app latency; retransmit storms ≈ packet loss; zero window ≈ slow receiver
TLS triage tree: no ServerHello = drop/block; alert at ClientHello = cipher/SNI mismatch; handshake OK then stall = MTU or app
Decrypt checklist: SSLKEYLOGFILE set → app restarted → capture during session → keylog loaded in Wireshark TLS prefs
Trade-off recap: capture filters trade flexibility for kernel efficiency; full captures trade disk/scale for completeness; decryption trades privacy for visibility
Trade-off recap 2: client-side capture shows what the user felt; server-side shows what the app did — latency truth lives in the difference
Automation: tshark -r cap.pcap -Y 'tcp.analysis.retransmission' -T fields -e frame.time -e ip.src for scripted retransmit reports
Five-question checklist: Where captured? What filter? Clocks synced? Both sides? Keys available?
Final takeaway: packets don't lie — the wire is ground truth; capture wide, filter late, time everything, and always compare both ends
